# Surprise-Guided MergeSort: Budget-Efficient Human-in-the-Loop Ranking via Adaptive Comparison Scheduling

**Abstract.** Pairwise comparison is the gold standard for subjective ranking tasks; however, exhaustive annotation requires a massive number of human comparisons (_O(n_<sup>2</sup>)). While sorting-based methods have reduced this burden to _O(n_log_n_), they still require expensive human judgment for every single comparison. To further improve annotation efficiency, we propose leveraging a Vision–Language Model (VLM) not as an annotator replacement, but as a _question prioritizer_ to identify which comparisons genuinely require human judgment. The proposed **Surprise-Guided MergeSort (SGS)** method centers on a Round-0 _calibrated gating_ step: a small set of human comparisons estimates VLM–human agreement, which both decides whether the VLM ordering is trustworthy enough to drive a sorting backbone and initializes an agreement-aware Elo warm start. On top of this gate, SGS adopts a standard bottom-up MergeSort schedule and contributes the budget-aware integration of (i) a composite Surprise Scorer--combining position-bias-cancelled VLM confidence, Elo gap, and vote entropy--and (ii) a progress-capped automatic-resolution rule, so that high-surprise pairs are routed to humans while low-surprise pairs are resolved automatically. Validation was conducted on six diverse benchmarks spanning text similarity and image quality assessment. SGS automatically resolves up to 535 low-surprise edges per session and achieves Kendall’s \(\tau\times 100\) gains of +6 to +12 over Active Elo on datasets where the VLM pre-ordering is directionally useful. A controlled simulation with multi-seed confidence intervals measures inferred-edge accuracy and shows that the method falls back toward warm-started Active Elo when the VLM prior is globally unreliable.

**Keywords:** Pairwise Ranking \(\cdot\) Human-in-the-Loop \(\cdot\) Active Learning \(\cdot\) MergeSort \(\cdot\) VLM \(\cdot\) Annotation Efficiency

### 1 Introduction

Pairwise comparison provides more reliable supervision than absolute ratings for subjective annotation tasks [2,24], yielding higher inter-rater agreement across domains from medical imaging to text similarity assessment. However, the

Yujin Park<sup>1</sup> , Haejun Chung<sup>1(<sup>\(\boxtimes\)</sup>)</sup>, and Ikbeom Jang<sup>2(<sup>\(\boxtimes\)</sup>)</sup>

<sup>1</sup> Hanyang University, Seoul, Republic of Korea `{yujin1019a,haejun}@hanyang.ac.kr`

<sup>2</sup> Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, Yongin, Republic of Korea `ijang@hufs.ac.kr`

<tbc>quadratic cost of exhaustive comparison (_O(n_<sup>2</sup>)) makes it impractical at scale: ranking 200 items requires nearly 20,000 comparisons, each demanding seconds of expert time.

Sorting-based approaches reduce the comparison count to _O(n_log_n_) by embedding pairwise queries within a sorting algorithm [14,9]. Recent work further leverages pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) to provide coarse initial orderings, enabling the sorting procedure to skip trivially resolvable pairs [17,10,16]. Despite this progress, a fundamental tension remains: VLM predictions are noisy--particularly for fine-grained distinctions where items have similar quality scores--yet existing methods either trust VLM outputs as-is or require human judgment for every comparison the sort requests.

We identify three limitations of current approaches. First, VLM-as-annotator methods [20] suffer from position bias and limited accuracy on near-tie pairs, with typical agreement rates of 60-70% against human judgment. Second, purely human sorting methods [9,14] waste budget on easy comparisons where VLM ordering is reliable. Third, ensemble-based approaches [17] introduce substantial computational overhead from neural ranking heads and Gaussian Process inference, limiting scalability to larger item sets.

We propose **Surprise-Guided MergeSort (SGS)**, which reframes the VLM’s role from annotator to _question prioritizer_. Rather than trusting or replacing VLM decisions, SGS measures how _surprised_ the system is by each proposed comparison and allocates the limited human budget to the most ambiguous pairs. The key insight is that a comparison is "surprising" when multiple uncertainty signals--VLM confidence after position-bias cancellation, Elo rating gap, and annotator vote entropy--all indicate genuine ambiguity. Low-surprise comparisons are automatically resolved under a capped inference policy and then propagated through the MergeSort transitive closure.

This design philosophy aligns with recent findings in active ranking for scientific imaging [18], where VLM priors are used only to guide informative sampling rather than as ground-truth annotations. A Round-0 calibration gate keeps SGS robust to _globally_ unreliable priors: when measured VLM-human agreement falls below 70%, SGS disables the sorting backbone and reverts to a warm-started Active Elo, preventing error propagation from a misleading initial ordering (we analyze the gate’s behavior, including its limits, in Section 5).

In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

**1. Agreement-calibrated VLM use.** SGS estimates VLM-human agreement \(\alpha\) from a small calibration set and uses it for both a centeredness-banded Elo warm start and an explicit gate: the MergeSort backbone is used only when the measured prior is sufficiently reliable; otherwise the method falls back to warm- started Active Elo. **2. Surprise-guided comparison routing.** SGS adopts a standard bottom-up MergeSort backbone and adds a budget-allocation layer that combines position-bias-cancelled VLM uncertainty, Elo-gap uncertainty, and vote entropy. High-surprise boundary pairs are sent to humans, while low-surprise pairs are admitted only under a progress-capped automatic-resolution policy.

<tbc>**3. Domain-level diagnostics.** Across six benchmarks and a controlled simulation, we show that SGS is strongest when the VLM provides a coarse but directionally useful pre-ordering. We also identify failure modes where graph-based exploration remains preferable, especially when aggregate calibration agreement hides errors on hard near-tie pairs.

### 2 Related Work

#### 2.1 Pairwise Ranking and Sorting-Based Annotation

The Bradley-Terry model [2] provides a principled foundation for pairwise comparison, estimating item quality from binary preference data. Sorting-based active learning reduces annotation cost from _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) to _O(n_log_n_) by querying only the pairs needed to complete a sort [9,14]. PairS [10] applies merge sort to LLM-based ranking with uncertainty-guided pair selection, demonstrating strong performance on text benchmarks. Recent theoretical analysis [11] examines the optimality of comparison-based sorting when individual comparisons are handled by language models.

#### 2.2 VLM-Assisted Ranking

Large-scale VLMs such as CLIP [21] and multimodal LLMs support zero-shot quality ordering via text prompts. EZ-Sort [16] combines CLIP-based hierarchical pre-ordering with uncertainty-aware MergeSort and achieves substantial annotation reduction on small datasets. SGS is closest to this line of work, as it also uses VLM-derived pre-ordering, MergeSort scheduling, and uncertainty-based skipping of easy pairs. We therefore do not claim MergeSort scheduling itself as the primary novelty. Instead, SGS adds an agreement-calibrated control layer: Round-0 human-VLM agreement determines whether the sorting backbone is used, VLM scores warm-start Elo only under conservative agreement-dependent bands, and candidate pairs are routed by a composite surprise score before capped automatic resolution. Dodgersort [17] also uses model-derived ranking evidence, but refines automation through a neural ranking head and a probabilistic ensemble involving GP, Elo, and BTL components. SGS instead keeps a single Elo state and lightweight VLM scoring, trading ensemble complexity for calibration-gated routing and conservative fallback. MetaRanker [18] similarly treats VLM outputs as informative priors rather than ground-truth labels; SGS operationalizes this principle through calibrated routing and capped automatic resolution.

#### 2.3 Active Learning for Preference Ranking

Active preference learning minimizes annotation cost by querying maximally informative pairs. Information-theoretic approaches select pairs with highest expected information gain [4,7]. GURO [1] combines multiple uncertainty signals for robust pair selection. RAIR [12] uses Laplacian-based effective resistance to<tbc>

<tbc>measure pair informativeness within comparison graphs. These methods assume every selected pair requires human input. SGS differs by additionally classifying each candidate as human-required or transitivity-resolvable based on its surprise score.

### 2.4 Position Bias in LLM Comparisons

LLMs and VLMs exhibit systematic position bias in pairwise comparison tasks \[22,25\], where the order in which items are presented affects the output. The flip test--querying both orderings (_A,B_) and (_B,A_)--is a standard mitigation. We incorporate a calibrated version of the flip test as one component of our Surprise Score, converting position-bias-cancelled confidence into a continuous uncertainty signal.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Problem Setup

Let X={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_} be a set of items with unknown latent scores \(\{s_i\}_{i=1}^n\). The goal is to recover a ranking \(\hat{\mathcal{R}}\) that is maximally consistent with the ground-truth ordering while minimizing the number of _human_ pairwise judgments. We assume access to two complementary supervision channels: (i) a noisy VLM-based scorer that can assign pointwise scores to individual items and produce noisy pairwise preferences, and (ii) a reliable human oracle that returns the comparison outcome \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) for a queried pair (_i,j_).

Our design principle is to use the VLM as a _question prioritizer_ rather than as an annotator replacement. Accordingly, the VLM is used to (a) construct an initial coarse ordering, (b) estimate which comparisons are ambiguous, and (c) support low-risk automatic resolution. Human effort is reserved for comparisons whose ambiguity is high enough that automatic resolution is likely to be unreliable.

### 3.2 Method Overview

SGS first calibrates the VLM against a small set of human comparisons and uses the resulting agreement to warm-start an Elo state. When agreement is sufficient, a bottom-up MergeSort scheduler proposes local cross-run candidate pairs, which are scored by a composite surprise metric. High-surprise pairs are sent to humans, while low-surprise pairs are resolved only under a capped automatic-resolution policy; otherwise, the method falls back to Active Elo. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

### 3.3 Round-0 Calibration, Pre-Scoring, and Warm Start

_Calibration._ We first draw _n_<sub>cal</sub> unique random pairs and query both the VLM and the human oracle. Let \(\tilde{y}_{ij}\) denote the VLM decision and _y<sub>ij</sub>_ the human

<tbc>decision. Their agreement rate is

\(\alpha=\frac{1}{n_\mathrm{cal}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{C}_0}\mathbf{1}[\tilde{y}_{ij}=y_{ij}].\) (1)

This step serves two purposes: it estimates whether the VLM-derived ordering is trustworthy enough to support MergeSort, and it initializes Elo ratings from reliable human comparisons before any inference is attempted.

_Pointwise VLM pre-scoring._ For each item _x<sub>i</sub>_, the VLM is queried _K_ times with prompt perturbations or simulated annotator diversity, producing pointwise scores \(\{v_i^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K\). We define the mean pre-score as

\(\bar{v}_i=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^Kv_i^{(k)}.\) (2)

The initial order \(\pi_0\) is obtained by sorting items according to \(\bar{v}_i\) from worst to best.

_Agreement-aware Elo warm start._ The code applies an agreement-conditioned warm start rather than directly trusting the VLM scores. Let

\(z_i=2\left(\frac{\bar{v}_i-v_\mathrm{min}}{v_\mathrm{max}-v_\mathrm{min}+\varepsilon}-\frac{1}{2}\right),c_i=\frac{|\bar{v}_i-\mathrm{median}(\bar{v})|}{v_\mathrm{max}-v_\mathrm{min}+\varepsilon},\) (3)

where \(z_i\in[-1,1]\) is the centered normalized pre-score and _c<sub>i</sub>_ measures how far item _i_ lies from the ambiguous center of the score distribution. Because all three trusted cases share the same value, the warm start reduces to a single _banded_ gate: an item inherits VLM structure only if its centeredness _c<sub>i</sub>_ clears an agreement-dependent threshold \(\tau(\alpha)\),

\(R_i^{(0)}=1500+250z_i\cdot\mathbf{1}[c_i\ge\tau(\alpha)],\tau(\alpha)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
0, & \alpha\ge 0.70, \\
0.3, & 0.60\le\alpha<0.70, \\
0.5, & \alpha<0.60.
\end{array}\right.\) (4)

The band widens (higher \(\tau\)) as agreement drops, so when the VLM is less trustworthy only items far from the ambiguous center--where even a noisy prior is likely directionally correct--inherit a non-neutral rating; everyone else starts at 1500. The final Round-0 Elo state is then blended with the ratings accumulated from calibration comparisons:

\(R_i\leftarrow 0.5R_i+0.5R_i^{(0)}.\) (5)

This conservative blending limits anchoring by imperfect VLM priors while still injecting useful global structure.

M.getRanking() ### Adaptive fallback. Warm-starting is always performed, but the MergeSort backbone is only used when the calibration agreement is sufficiently high. If \(\alpha<0.70\), SGS abandons MergeSort and switches to Active Elo for all remaining rounds. This prevents a poor pre-order from inducing cascading errors in later merge passes. ## 3.4 Transitivity-Aware MergeSort Scheduler When \(\alpha\ge 0.70\), SGS initializes a bottom-up MergeSort scheduler from the VLM order \(\pi_0\). At each pass, only cross-run boundary pairs are considered, preserving the _O(n_log_n_) structure while avoiding global pair enumeration. The scheduler maintains a directed set K of reliable outcomes obtained from human labels or admitted inference, and skips pairs implied by the transitive closure of K. During pass completion, known relations are respected first; unresolved pairs are decided by Elo only when the rating gap is large (default \(|R_i-R_j|\ge 60\)), otherwise by the inherited run order. Transitivity is propagated only from reliable edges, not from weak VLM defaults.

### 3.5 Composite Surprise Score

The surprise score estimates the risk of resolving a pair without a human label. For each candidate pair (_i,j_), SGS computes three normalized uncertainty signals. First, forward and reverse VLM queries yield a position-bias-cancelled preference estimate,<tbc>

\(p_\text{fwd}=\frac{\mu_i^\rightarrow}{\mu_i^\rightarrow+\mu_j^\rightarrow+\varepsilon},p_\text{rev}=\frac{\mu_i^\leftarrow}{\mu_i^\leftarrow+\mu_j^\leftarrow+\varepsilon},\hat{p}_{ij}=\frac{p_\text{fwd}+p_\text{rev}}{2},\) (6)

<tbc>which is converted to VLM uncertainty \(S_\text{vlm}(i,j)=1-2|\hat{p}_{ij}-0.5|\). Second, the Elo gap \(\Delta_{ij}=|R_i-R_j|\) is mapped to<tbc>

\(S_\text{elo}(i,j)=1-2\left(\frac{1}{1+10^{-\Delta_{ij}/400}}-0.5\right).\) (7)

<tbc>Third, vote entropy _S_ent is computed from the _K_ simulated VLM votes. The final score is

\(S(i,j)=w_\text{vlm}S_\text{vlm}(i,j)+w_\text{elo}S_\text{elo}(i,j)+w_\text{ent}S_\text{ent}(i,j),\) (8)

with default weights (0.4,0.3,0.3).

### 3.6 Budget Allocation and Capped Automatic Resolution

At round _t_, the scheduler returns cross-run candidates whose outcomes are not already implied by transitivity. If more than 3_B_ unknown candidates are visible, SGS subsamples at most 3_B_ for surprise scoring, keeping VLM query cost linear in the round budget. The scored candidates are sorted by decreasing surprise. Pairs with \(S(i,j)\ge\theta_S\) are routed to the human oracle up to budget _B_; if fewer than _B_ pairs clear the threshold, the remaining budget is filled by the next most surprising pairs.

Low-surprise pairs are not automatically trusted wholesale. They are merely eligible for capped automatic resolution, with the cap reduced in later merge passes and under lower observed agreement:

\(C_t=max\left(20\cdot\mathbf{1}[\gamma_t>0],\text{round}(C_\text{max}\gamma_t)\right),\gamma_t=(1-0.7p_t)\big((1-\omega)+\omega\tilde{a}_t\big),\) (9)

where _p<sub>t</sub>_ is normalized merge-pass progress and \(\tilde{a}_t\) combines Round-0 agreement with the previous round’s human agreement. For an admitted pair, SGS uses Elo only when the rating gap is sufficiently informative (default \(|R_i-R_j|\ge 50\)). If VLM reliability is low, scheduler-order fallback is disabled and only high- confidence Elo decisions can support automatic resolution. In the reported experiments, inferred edges use _k_inf=0: they constrain pass completion and the transitive closure, but never update Elo, which is updated exclusively from human labels.

### 3.7 Round Completion, Recalibration, and Fallback Refinement

After human and admitted inferred edges have been processed, SGS completes the current merge pass and doubles the run size. The accumulated human labels can be used for lightweight test-time recalibration of the VLM-to-human mapping, improving later surprise estimates without replacing the surprise score. Two fallback behaviors are used: if Round-0 calibration yields \(\alpha<0.70\), SGS runs warm-started Active Elo for all remaining rounds; if all merge passes finish before the budget is exhausted, the remaining budget is spent on Active-Elo boundary refinement rather than redundant merge operations.

### 3.8 Complexity

Round-0 calibration uses _n_<sub>cal</sub> human comparisons and _Kn_ pointwise VLM scores. The structural comparison schedule induced by bottom-up MergeSort remains _O(n_log_n_) \[14,9,10\]. SGS does not alter this backbone; instead, it partitions the structural candidates into human-queried and automatically resolved subsets. Therefore, the total number of structurally considered pairs remains _O(n_log_n_), while the number of human comparisons is reduced to the subset of high-surprise pairs plus any Active Elo fallback rounds. In practice, the additional VLM pairwise cost is controlled by scoring at most 3_B_ candidates per round, which makes the ambiguity estimation stage linear in the round budget rather than quadratic in _n_.

### VLM query cost.

The total number of VLM calls is dominated by two terms: _Kn_ pointwise pre-scores in Round 0 and two pairwise calls (forward and reverse, for position-bias cancellation) for each of the \(\le 3B\) scored candidates per round. The session total is therefore at most _Kn_+6_BT_ VLM calls, independent of _n_<sup>2</sup>. Under our defaults (_K_=5, _n_=200, _B_=100, _T_=5) this is \(\le 1000+3000=4000\) calls per ranking session, all on a single pointwise/pairwise prompt template that admits caching and batching \[11\]. This is markedly cheaper than ensemble pipelines that invoke several neural models plus Gaussian-Process inference per decision \[17\], and--unlike human annotation--these calls are non-expert and parallelizable. We note that this cost is the main practical prerequisite of SGS: in domains where even pointwise VLM scoring is unavailable or unreliable, the method reduces to its Active-Elo fallback.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

### Datasets.

We evaluate on six benchmarks spanning two domains. For **text similarity**: STS-B \[3\] (test, 1,379 pairs), BIOSSES \[23\] (train, 100 biomedical pairs), and SICKR-STS (test, from MTEB \[15\], 4,906 pairs). For **image quality assessment**: KonIQ-10k \[6\] (train, 200 sampled images), TID2013 \[19\] (train, 200 sampled distorted images), and LIVE Challenge \[5\] (train, 200 sampled images). All scores are normalized to \[0,100\].

### VLM annotator.

We use Ollama-hosted Qwen-3.5 with _K_=5 simulated annotators per item providing pointwise quality scores via JSON-formatted prompts.

### Human oracle.

Following standard practice \[17,10\], we simulate the human oracle as \(h(i,j)=\mathbf{1}[s_i+\epsilon_i>s_j+\epsilon_j]\) where \(\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,25)\).

### Baselines.

We compare against five methods under identical total budget (\(n_\mathrm{cal}+T\times B=600\)): (1) **Random Elo**: random pair selection with Elo updates; (2) **Active Elo** \[8\]: Elo-gap-based active pair selection; (3) **Active Elo (same budget)**: Active Elo restricted to the same human budget as SGS; (4) **RAIR- Laplacian** \[12\]: Laplacian effective resistance pair selection; (5) **PairS-like MergeSort** \[10\]: PairS-style merge sort with VLM-gap-based uncertainty.

### Default hyperparameters.

All hyperparameters and their rationale are listed in  1; they are held fixed across all six datasets (no per-dataset tuning). The surprise weights (0.4,0.3,0.3) slightly favor the VLM-confidence term as the only signal available before any human label is collected; the sensitivity of the results to \(\theta_S\) and \(\alpha\) is examined in Section 4.5.

### 4.4 Per-Signal Surprise Ablation

We disentangle the three surprise signals on the real VLM using cached Qwen-3.5 scores and 10 seeds on BIOSSES and STS-B ( 4). Removing the Elo-gap term hurts most on both datasets, indicating that the human-derived ranking state-- initialized by Round-0 warm start--is the most useful signal. The VLM-confidence term is domain-dependent: it helps on STS-B, where the VLM pre-order is strong, but hurts on BIOSSES, where dropping it improves both \(\tau\) and inferred accuracy. The fixed composite is therefore a robust default rather than a tuned optimum; learned or agreement-dependent weights are a natural extension.

### 4.5 Controlled Simulation: Diagnostics and Ablations

To obtain multi-seed uncertainty estimates and ground-truth inferred-edge accuracy, we complement the fixed-VLM benchmarks with a controlled simulation in which the VLM annotator is replaced by a synthetic pointwise scorer whose agreement \(\alpha\) is tuned by noise \(\sigma_v\). We use _n_=200, the default budget, and report 10-seed means with 95% bootstrap CIs ( 5); absolute \(\tau\) values are not comparable to the VLM benchmarks.

As \(\alpha\) falls, the fallback rate rises from 0% to 70% and the inferred ratio shrinks from 47% to 14%, showing controlled degradation toward warm-started Active Elo under globally unreliable priors. Holding \(\alpha\approx 0.80\), removing the warm start reduces \(\tau\times 100\) from 62.7 to 49.2, whereas removing transitivity propagation leaves accuracy statistically unchanged while eliminating the edge multiplier. Thus, warm start drives accuracy; the MergeSort closure mainly improves budget efficiency.

## 5 Discussion

### When the budget multiplier helps.

The edge multiplier is most valuable when two conditions hold: the VLM pre-ordering is directionally correct, and the human budget alone is insufficient to saturate the ranking. LIVE-C and STS-B satisfy both conditions and show the largest gains. KonIQ is different: Random Elo already reaches 65.5 with 600 comparisons, close to SGS at 65.8, so additional inferred edges yield diminishing returns.

### Domain reliability and failure modes.

SGS is not a universal replacement for graph- based active ranking. Image IQA often provides coarse perceptual cues that VLMs capture, while semantic similarity can require fine compositional judgments that weaken pointwise VLM scoring. On SICKR-STS, Random Elo slightly exceeds SGS (63.9 vs. 63.5), suggesting that MergeSort boundary constraints can be uninformative when \(\pi_0\) is miscalibrated. The likely issue is that \(\alpha\ge 0.70\) may be concentrated on easy pairs; the binary gate then passes although hard near-tie pairs remain unreliable. A soft fallback that mixes MergeSort candidates with graph/random exploration, or a per-round agreement check, would address this limitation.

### Limitations and reproducibility.

The six VLM benchmarks are single-seed; the controlled simulation supplies bootstrap CIs and inferred-edge diagnostics, but multi-seed VLM runs remain needed for marginal cases such as KonIQ. The Gaussian simulated oracle does not capture systematic human effects such as fatigue or anchoring. The surprise weights and \(\alpha=0.70\) gate are fixed defaults rather than learned. All six benchmarks are public, and we release the reference implementation, seed list, hyperparameters, controlled-simulation harness, and real-VLM ablation scripts used to reproduce the reported diagnostics.

## 6 Conclusion

We presented SGS, a budget-efficient pairwise-ranking method that treats VLMs as question prioritizers rather than annotator replacements. The main mechanism is an agreement-calibrated Round-0 gate with a banded Elo warm start; a standard MergeSort backbone then exposes local boundary pairs, which SGS routes using composite surprise and capped automatic resolution. Across six benchmarks,<tbc>

# Surprise-Guided MergeSort

<tbc>SGS achieves the best average \(\tau\times 100\) while adding up to a 47% edge multiplier; controlled diagnostics show that these inferred edges are useful but imperfect, and that the method degrades toward warm-started Active Elo when the VLM prior is globally unreliable.

The empirical picture is domain-dependent: SGS is strongest when VLM pre-ordering is directionally informative, especially for perceptual IQA, while graph-based methods remain preferable on some semantic-similarity tasks. Future work should replace the binary agreement gate with soft or per-round fallback, learn surprise weights from calibration data, and validate the method with real annotators.
